title: Human nutrient turnover evidence and intake-history model
scope: Healthy adult reference evidence; not individual pharmacokinetics or a clinical reserve estimate.
model: For supported nutrients, retain each recorded day's capped target-equivalent intake with r^ageDays. r=1-lossFractionPerDay or 2^(-1/halfLifeDays). Sum in target-days. Initial body stores are unknown and are not inferred. Daily modes count today's intake only; this is a reporting rule, not a biological half-life.
limitations: Half-life, time to deficiency, plasma biomarker turnover and whole-body turnover are different quantities.
Applying a population turnover coefficient to dietary intake is a transparent visualization assumption, not a validated estimate of absorption or body stores.
Each day's contribution is capped at one daily target to avoid treating high intake as unlimited stored credit. This cap is a product rule, not a physiological storage capacity.
A missing food-log day means no recorded contribution, not proven fasting. Missing food nutrient values remain unknown.
Rates depend on nutrient status, compartment, intake, absorption, recycling and health. Unsupported nutrients have no invented half-life.

calories.summary: Daily energy budget; energy can be expended or stored. There is no universal calorie half-life.
calories.reason: Daily reset is a tracking convention, not disappearance of body energy.

protein.summary: Daily intake target. Protein turnover varies between tissues and cannot be represented by an oral-intake half-life.
protein.reason: No universal body-protein decay constant used.

carbs.summary: Daily intake target. Carbohydrate can be oxidized or contribute to energy stores.
carbs.reason: No universal dietary-carbohydrate decay constant used.

fat.summary: Daily intake target. Dietary fat can be expended or stored; it does not expire at midnight.
fat.reason: Daily reset is a tracking convention.

fiber.summary: Daily intake target; dietary fiber is not a replenishable body nutrient reserve.

vitaminA.evidence: Approximately 0.5% of total stores lost daily in adults on a vitamin-A-free diet.
vitaminA.selection: Use the reported fractional loss; derived exponential half-time is about 138.3 days.
vitaminA.summary: 0.5% daily store loss in depletion studies; applying it to intake is a model assumption.

vitaminC.evidence: Reported biological half-life varies from 8 to 40 days with body pool and intake.
vitaminC.selection: 24 days is the arithmetic midpoint chosen for display; it is not a measured universal half-life.
vitaminC.summary: 8–40 day range; model uses a 24-day midpoint. Strong homeostatic dependence.

vitaminD.compartment: Circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D, not dietary D2/D3 or total stores
vitaminD.summary: The 15-day half-life describes blood 25(OH)D, not loss of a dietary vitamin D serving.
vitaminD.reason: The food log cannot map sunlight, conversion and tissue stores to this biomarker. No dietary turnover coefficient applied.

vitaminE.summary: Circulating concentrations and dietary intake do not map reliably to one body-store turnover rate.
vitaminE.reason: No universal whole-body half-life adopted from the reviewed source.

vitaminK.summary: Rapid metabolism, small stores and different K forms; a single intake-decay constant is not established here.
vitaminK.reason: No invented numeric half-life; daily intake remains visible.

b1.evidence: The DRI review gives an estimated biological half-life of 9 to 18 days.
b1.selection: 13.5 days is the arithmetic midpoint of the cited range, selected for the visualization.
b1.summary: 9–18 day estimated range; model uses a 13.5-day midpoint.

b2.summary: Only small amounts are stored and excess is excreted. The reviewed source does not establish one whole-body half-life.
b2.reason: Daily intake shown without a guessed rate.

b6.compartment: Estimated overall body B6 in historical tracer models
b6.evidence: Historical tracer models estimated an overall body half-life around 25 days; the DRI review questions whether slow muscle pools were adequately represented.
b6.selection: Use 25 days as a provisional population-model coefficient with the source's compartment caveat.
b6.summary: About 25 days in a questioned historical model; individual turnover differs.

b12.compartment: Whole-body B12 pool with enterohepatic recycling
b12.evidence: Studies reviewed by the National Academies report 0.1–0.2% daily loss of the B12 pool; 0.2% can reflect impaired biliary reabsorption.
b12.selection: Use 0.1% daily loss for the healthy-adult reference. Derived half-time is about 692.8 days; this is not time to deficiency.
b12.summary: 0.1% daily reference loss; derived half-time about 693 days. Unknown starting stores and absorption.

folate.summary: Fast and slow folate pools span hours to more than 100 days; one fixed constant would hide this compartment difference.
folate.reason: No single whole-body dietary coefficient applied.

calcium.summary: Most body calcium is in bone; ongoing remodeling and homeostasis prevent a single daily-food decay model.
calcium.reason: Daily intake reporting; no mineral disappearance rate.

iron.summary: Iron is recycled; losses and needs differ with blood loss and other factors.
iron.reason: No universal iron half-life applied to food logs.

magnesium.summary: Bone, cells and kidney regulation create multiple pools and variable losses.
magnesium.reason: No single body-store decay coefficient adopted.

zinc.summary: Intake, absorption and excretion determine balance; the reviewed guidance does not give a universal dietary half-life.
zinc.reason: Daily intake reporting without a guessed rate.

potassium.summary: Intracellular distribution and renal regulation govern potassium balance.
